# Holo-NN: Holographic Nearest Neighbor Search via Compressive Sensing

### Abstract

In the age of AI, privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search over high-dimensional embeddings has emerged as a critical yet frustratingly challenging domain, dominated by tradeoffs between speed, privacy, and accuracy. Traditional tree and graph-based indexing structures (e.g., HNSW, ScaNN) rely fundamentally on non-linear operations that are computationally intractable under Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) or blind server-side constraints.

In this paper, we introduce **Holo-NN** (**Holographic Nearest Neighbor Search**), an algebraic framework that replaces data-dependent branching with a single linear projection. Our key observation is that while distances across a database are dense, neighborhood membership is inherently sparse: only a handful of points ever lie close to a query. By pairing locality-preserving feature transforms with Compressive Sensing, Holo-NN folds the entire database offline into a compact holographic sensing matrix. At query time, encrypted search reduces to a single, non-interactive matrix-vector multiplication--requiring no FHE bootstrapping, no multi-round interaction, and no client-side index state. This turns private retrieval into an embarrassingly parallel, accuracy-tunable computation that runs out of the box on both CPUs and GPUs, scaling efficiently to production databases. We offer a comparison against other state-of-the-art Private ANN algorithms to help situate the method in the broader context of production-grade private retrieval.

### 1 Introduction

#### 1.1 Motivation & Private Retrieval Landscape

Published in 1750, Cramer’s rule [19] established an exceptionally inefficient and computationally intensive method for solving systems of linear equations based on an exhaustive calculation of determinants. And yet, despite its inefficiency, it introduced an embarrassingly parallel mathematical primitive that modern high-throughput computational hardware can execute with extreme efficiency.

A similar paradigm shift governs modern privacy-

preserving computation. The constraints imposed by fully end-to-end secure computation--such as Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) and Private Information Retrieval (PIR)--fundamentally alter algorithmic tradeoffs, introducing choices that would be sub-optimal in most other settings. In unconstrained plaintext environments, Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search is dominated by hierarchical graphs (e.g., HNSW [35]) and quantized inverted files (e.g., ScaNN [28]), which exploit non-linear geometric branching to achieve sublinear query times (O(log_N_) for hierarchical graphs such as HNSW). In contrast, in private, blind-server settings, data-dependent branching leaks memory access patterns, rendering graph traversals either insecure, reliant on non-colluding multi-server assumptions (e.g., PRECO [40]), or subject to heavy multi-round cryptographic overheads across garbled circuits, oblivious RAM, or sublinear PIR (e.g., SANNS [14], Tiptoe [29], Pacmann [48], Panther [32], Compass [49]). Under strict single-server privacy constraints, non-interactive systems are forced into an O(_N_) linear scan of the entire database. When server compute and memory capacity are abundant relative to communication bandwidth and cryptographic circuit depth, algorithm design shifts toward strictly linear, non-interactive mathematical formulations.

#### 1.2 Compressed Sensing

Beginning with Claerbout and Muir in 1973 [18], it was discovered that seismological reflection data could be algorithmically improved, even with apparent "violations" of the Nyquist-Shannon sampling criterion [41]. Formalized later into the robust field of Compressive Sensing, it was shown that the supposed violation was backed by the inherent sparsity of the underlying signals [22, 10]. Specifically, for a signal that admits a _k_- sparse representation where \(k\checkmark N\), significantly fewer measurements than _N_ are required for high-fidelity reconstruction. Intuitively, reconstruction is possible because one is attempting to solve for _k_ non-zero elements in an _N_-dimensional space, which can be solved efficiently via convex \(\ell_1\)-optimization algorithms. Formally, given an underdetermined system of linear measurements \(y=As\in\mathbb{R}^M\) with \(M\checkmark N\), an unknown _k_-sparse signal \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) can be recovered by solving the convex program \(min_s\left\|s\right\|_1\) subject to _As=y_ (or \(\left\|As-y\right\|_2\le\epsilon\) under

Compressive Sensing has since enjoyed a long series of successes in Signal Processing \[12, 5, 34\], though has become more of a background player in modern systems design, and it is rare to see application outside of practical acquisition systems like single-pixel optical imaging \[26\], Astronomy \[7\], WiFi or wireless sensor networks \[4\], to name a few.

In classical Compressive Sensing, a signal \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\) (e.g., an image in JPEG \[44\]) admits a _k_-sparse representation \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) under a sparsifying basis or dictionary \(F\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) such that _x=Fs_. Instead of acquiring all _N_ ambient samples and compressing them post hoc, compressive sensing directly acquires \(M\checkmark N\) non-adaptive linear measurements via a pseudorandom measurement matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}\):

\(y=Ax=AFs\) (1)

The sparse coefficient vector _s_ is then reconstructed from _y_ by applying convex \(\ell_1\)-regularized recovery algorithms \[42, 6, 43, 21, 15\], after which the original signal _x=Fs_ can be synthesized if needed.

In our nearest-neighbor setting (Section 1.3), the paradigm is even more direct: the sparse vector \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) is _itself_ the primary object of interest. Specifically, _s_ is the database affinity vector whose coordinates indicate the nearest neighbors of a query. Consequently, recovering _s_ directly from compressed measurements _y=As_ immediately reveals the nearest-neighbor candidates (and their approximate distances) without requiring secondary reconstruction of an underlying signal _x_. Because _A_ is pseudorandom and the database features are known _a priori_, the server’s linear operator can be precomputed offline, leaving only the compact vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^M\) to be transmitted to the client.

## 1.3 Nearest Neighbor Search as Sparse Signal Recovery

Consider a database \(T=\{t_1,t_2,\dots,t_N\}\subset\mathbb{R}^D\) of _N_ vectors and a query point \(q\in\mathbb{R}^D\). For a nearest-neighbor query we are interested in the domain of distances from the query point to the points in the database, most specifically with the closest point. While the pairwise distance vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^N\) with entries _d<sub>i</sub>_=dist(_q,t<sub>i</sub>_) is completely dense, the corresponding _k_-nearest neighbor indicator vector \(s\in\{0,1\}^N\) is, by construction, exactly _k_-sparse. In particular, for 1-NN retrieval, _s_ is a 1-hot vector containing a single non-zero entry among _N_ coordinates.

From this perspective, nearest neighbor search can be cast as the recovery of a sparse affinity signal from compressed linear projections. In our formulation, the target signal \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) is not merely an uninformative binary 0/1 indicator, but a continuous _local affinity vector_ whose entries _s<sub>i</sub>_=sim(_q,t<sub>i</sub>_) concentrate their mass within the query’s local Voronoi neighborhood. This continuous mass is a key feature: its relative amplitudes preserve metric resolution and local ranking among adjacent points within<tbc>

<tbc>the cell (as visualized in Figure 2), while decaying rapidly to zero across distant background points to enforce effective sparsity.

The server compresses this affinity field into \(M\checkmark N\) linear measurements \(y=As\in\mathbb{R}^M\) via a pseudorandom measurement matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}\). The core challenge is designing feature embeddings F and G that guarantee that distances are meaningful, but that decay quickly enough such that _s_ is sufficiently sparse for stable Compressive Sensing recovery, allowing the server to compute _y=As_ without ever computing the full _N_-dimensional vector _s_.

While the raw query \(q\in\mathbb{R}^D\) is generally dense, and can be performed via linear operations simply (e.g., _d=u<sup>T</sup>u+v<sup>T</sup>v_-2(_u<sup>T</sup>v_) for vectors _u_ and _v_), modern machine learning provides effective non-linear feature embeddings that induce sparsity in an expanded feature space R_<sup>B</sup>_ (\(B\gg D\)). Specifically, Kernel Methods (e.g., Random Fourier Features \[36\]) and Locality Sensitive Hashing (e.g., FlyHash \[20\]) allow sparsified continuous metric distances to be approximated via linear inner products:

\(\mathrm{sim}(q,t_i)\approx\langle\mathcal{G}(t_i),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle\)

Where G and F are sparsity-enhancing feature transforms. By stacking the _N_ transformed database vectors into a database feature matrix \(G=\mathcal{G}(T)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times B}\), where row _i_ is G(_t<sub>i</sub>)<sup>T</sup>_, the uncompressed affinity vector \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) across the entire database is then simply the matrix-vector product:

\(s=GF(q)=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
\langle\mathcal{G}(t_1),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle \\
\vdots \\
\langle\mathcal{G}(t_N),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^N\) (2)

By pre-multiplying this database feature matrix by a pseudorandom measurement matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}\), we construct the **Holographic Sensing Matrix**:

\(H:=AG\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times B}\) (3)

It’s useful to pause and note the connection to Holography and physical intuition behind it. Specifically for an isolated vector pair \(\langle\mathcal{G}(t_i),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle\), _a priori_, the computation shares no information with any neighbors and<tbc>

<tbc>therefore the _s<sub>i</sub>_ would need to be exhaustively calculated for a full comparison. (This is the primary mechanism behind the proof that any sorting algorithm’s complexity floor is O(_N_log_N_)). In Holography, however, information in one basis is "smeared out" across a complementary basis (e.g., the Fourier Transform) ensuring that every sample contains fractional information about every point in the conjugate basis. Here _H_ plays this role, dispersing distances across multiple measurements that, collectively and in far fewer number than _N_, can infer the signal of interest.

The linear framing cleanly separates the problem into an offline precomputation and an online linear query evaluation:

\(y=H\mathcal{F}(q)=\left(AG\right)\mathcal{F}(q)=A\left(G\mathcal{F}(q)\right)=As\in\mathbb{R}^M\) (4)

Here, _H_ is computed once offline and stored permanently. Given a query F(_q_), the evaluator simply computes the linear product _y=H_F(_q_), producing the compressed measurements \(y\in\mathbb{R}^M\) without ever materializing the uncompressed _N_-dimensional vector _s_. The querier, knowing only the pseudorandom matrix _A_, can then recover the sparse affinity vector \(\hat{s}\) directly from _y=As_ via standard convex recovery algorithms (discussed below) in a fully local environment, without ever needing to know or download the holographic database matrix _H_.

Moreover, because of the lossy nature of the initial transform, we can, with judicious design of the matrix _A_, precisely control the accuracy of the final output and more importantly, allow for an algorithmically tunable tradeoff between accuracy and cost.

By synthesizing Compressive Sensing with non-linear feature embeddings, this forms the basis of **Holo-NN**, a strictly linear approximate nearest neighbor retrieval framework designed for regimes where server storage and parallel compute are inexpensive relative to network bandwidth and client storage, and both query privacy and index protection are paramount.

## 1.4 Summary of Contributions

1. **Holographic Retrieval tion**: We reformulate ANN search as a single-round-trip (1-RTT), non-interactive linear Compressive Sensing problem (_y=H_F(_q_)) utilizing an offline precomputed holographic matrix \(H=AG(T)\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times B}\).<tbc>

2. **Asymmetric Neural Hashing & Geometric Duality**: We characterize the manifold duality governing sparse feature lifting--showing why continuous Random Fourier Features sparsify spatial Euclidean manifolds while discrete hyperplane competition is required on high-dimensional semantic hyperspheres-- and introduce Asymmetric FlyHash (_k<sub>q</sub>\>k_db) to eliminate double-quantization dropouts at zero encrypted wire overhead (Section 4 and Section 5).<tbc>

3. **Multi-Backend Encrypted Implementation & SOTA Comparison**: We implement Holo-NN across four complementary cryptographic backends-- stateless exact-integer **LinPIR (BFV)** \[31\] on CPU (3.29 s across 4 cores or 4.39 s single-threaded on Wikipedia-500k, and 3.1-8.0 s of server compute across 6 cores on SIFT-1M, with zero server keys), depth-1 mod-switched **OpenFHE CKKS** \[1\] on CPU (1.60 MB wire), **Phantom CUDA CKKS** \[45\] on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (1.68 s end-to- end / 1.54 s server on Wikipedia-500k, and 9.5-29.7 s on SIFT-1M), and 32-bit RNS **HEIR/Cheddar CUDA CKKS** \[3, 17\] on a single RTX 3090 GPU (0.79 MB wire in 0.134 s end-to-end / 50.5 ms server on Wikipedia-500k, and 2.10-5.37 MB wire in 0.26-0.82 s on SIFT-1M)--and benchmark against SANNS \[14\], PRECO \[40\], Tiptoe \[29\], Pacmann \[48\], Panther \[32\], Compass \[49\], and Onyx \[37\] across all published recall conventions (2.10-11.13 MB CKKS wire on SIFT-1M in 1 RTT, 8.3\(\times\)-44.2\(\times\) below Panther’s 92.9 MB, 159\(\times\)-843\(\times\) below SANNS’s 1.77 GB, and below Compass’s 12.2 MB over 8 RTTs).<tbc>

## 2 Background & Problem tion

### 2.1 Threat Model & Security Setting

We consider a client-server architecture where an untrusted server S hosts a large-scale database \(T=\{t_1,t_2,\dots,t_N\}\subset\mathbb{R}^D\) of _N_ high-dimensional feature vectors, and a client holds a confidential query vector \(q\in\mathbb{R}^D\).

The objective is to retrieve the approximate nearest neighbor \(q^*=\mathrm{argmin}_{t_i\in T}\mathrm{dist}(q,t_i)\) under standard metric spaces--specifically Euclidean distance ∥_q-t<sub>i</sub>_∥<sub>2</sub> (e.g., via RFF) or angular cosine similarity \(\frac{\langle q,t_i\rangle}{\left\|q\right\|_2\left\|t_i\right\|_2}\) (e.g., via FlyHash)--subject to basic privacy constraints:

1. **Query & Access-Pattern Privacy**: Under standard IND-CPA Ring-LWE encryption, the server S learns nothing about the client’s query _q_. Crucially, unlike graph- or tree-based private search that leaks data-dependent branching paths, the server’s execution trace (_y=H_F(_q_)) is strictly _data-oblivious_: it touches every measurement channel uniformly in a single linear pass, and hence the holographic naming, eliminating memory access-pattern leakage.<tbc>

2. **Index Protection (Bounded Single-Query Leakage)**: The client never downloads the raw database _T_ or the holographic index _H_. For an honest- but-curious client issuing a query _q_, the single _M_- dimensional response \(y=A\mathcal{F}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^M\) (\(M\checkmark N\)) is an underdetermined linear projection with an (_N-M_)-dimensional null space in R_<sup>N</sup>_, enabling sparse recovery of the \(K^*\checkmark N\) local Voronoi neighbors without transmitting raw vectors _T_. Defending against an adaptive malicious client that issues O(_B_) chosen basis queries to reconstruct _H_ (or inspects ciphertext error terms) is orthogonal to our core primitive and requires standard query rate-limiting, noise flooding for circuit privacy, and zero-knowledge proofs of query well-formedness.<tbc>

3. **Operational Model**: We target deployment settings where server-side storage and high-throughput parallel compute are abundant, but client storage and network bandwidth across wide area networks (WAN) and multi-round cryptographic communication overheads are the dominant system bottlenecks.

### 2.2 Compressive Sensing & Restricted Isometry Property

Compressive Sensing \[22, 10, 27\] enables the stable, high probability, reconstruction of an _N_-dimensional sparse signal<tbc>

\(s\in\mathbb{R}^N(|\mathrm{support}(s)|\le k\checkmark N)\) (5)

<tbc>from an underdetermined measurement vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^M\) with \(M\checkmark N\) and support the number of non-zero entries:

\(y=As\) (6)

where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}\) is a measurement operator satisfying the **Restricted Isometry Property (RIP)** \[9, 11\] of order _k_. Specifically, there exists an isometry constant \(\delta_k\in(0,1)\) such that for all _k_-sparse vectors _s_:

\((1-\delta_k)\left\|s\right\|_2^2\le\left\|As\right\|_2^2\le(1+\delta_k)\left\|s\right\|_2^2\) (7)

In practice, _A_ is drawn from appropriately chosen random ensembles, most commonly:

\(A\in\{-1,+1\}^{M\times N}\text{(Bernoulli)}\) (8)

\(A\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{1}{M}\right)^{M\times N}\text{(Gaussian)}\) (9)

Though, given that Bernoulli amounts to random sums and negations of existing column entries, this distribution is typically the most efficient choice.

Because _A_ is pseudorandom, any entry (_i,j_) or column can be evaluated on the fly in O(1) time by both client and server using a Pseudorandom Function (PRF) _F<sub>k</sub>(i,j_) keyed by a compact shared seed _k_ (e.g., 128-bit AES-CTR), eliminating any requirement to transmit or materialize _A_ in memory or GPU VRAM.

### 2.3 Kernel Lifting & Distance Approximations

In metric nearest neighbor search, non-linear geometric distances (_L_<sub>2</sub> Euclidean distance or cosine similarity) can be directly evaluated via linear operations in the raw feature space R_<sup>D</sup>(u<sup>T</sup>u+v<sup>T</sup>v_-2_u<sup>T</sup>v_), but they are typically dense in _N_. To bridge this gap, feature mapping functions \(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}:\mathbb{R}^D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^B\) lift continuous vectors into an expanded _B_-dimensional space (\(B\gg D\)) where a localized similarity kernel sim(_q,t<sub>i</sub>_)--defined as a positive, monotonically decreasing function of metric distance dist(_q,t<sub>i</sub>_) that vanishes outside a local neighborhood--is preserved as a linear inner product:

\(\mathrm{sim}(q,t_i)\approx\langle\mathcal{F}(q),\mathcal{G}(t_i)\rangle\) (10)

While many kernel feature mappings exist, two are of particular use for our purposes:

1. **Gaussian Radial Basis Function via Random Fourier Features**: Approximating a radial distance function, Gaussian Radial Basis Function (RBF) \[39\] via Random Fourier Features (RFF) \[36\] allows _L_<sub>2</sub> minimization over a tunable radius without the need for an interactive rounding procedure. Via Bochner’s theorem \[8\], shift-invariant kernels such as the RBF \(K(x,y)=\mathrm{exp}(-\gamma\left\|x-y\right\|_2^2)\) are approximated by<tbc>

projecting vectors onto random Gaussian frequencies \(W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2\gamma I)\) to produce \(\mathbf{f}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^B\): \(\mathbf{f}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{B/2}}\left[\begin{array}{ c } cos(Wx) \\ sin(Wx) \end{array}\right]\) \(\text{(11)}\) The RBF acts as a spatial bandpass filter: points within a Euclidean radius \(\propto 1/\sqrt{\gamma}\) produce positive inner products, while distant points decay exponentially toward zero, inducing physical sparsity. 2. **FlyHash (Biologically Inspired Sparse Hashing)**: Serving as an angular analog to the Euclidean RBF, FlyHash \[20\] has frequently \[33, 38\] been used to approximate cosine similarity across directional semantic embeddings. Inspired by the _Drosophila_ olfactory circuit \[13\], continuous vectors are projected onto random sparse binary hyperplanes \(W\in\{0,1\}^{B\times D}\) and can be sparsified via winner-take-all (_k_-WTA) competitive inhibition to yield a binary code, as in traditional applications, or a sparse gated projection as in our work \(\mathbf{f}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^B\) whose _j_-th coordinate is: \(\mathbf{f}(x)_j=[\text{WTA}_k(Wx)]_j\)
\(=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } (Wx)_j & \text{if}(Wx)_j\in\text{Top-}k(Wx) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{array}\right.\) \(\text{(12)}\) Much like RBF creates localized hyperspheres in Euclidean space, FlyHash creates localized angular cones on the hypersphere, mapping angular proximity directly to the inner product overlap \(\langle\mathbf{f}(x),\mathbf{f}(y)\rangle\) of sparse representations while remaining resilient to high-dimensional metric concentration. Throughout the remainder of this paper, the query mapping \(\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{R}^D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^B\) and database mapping \(\mathcal{G}:\mathbb{R}^D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^B\) denote these localized feature liftings--instantiated via RFF for Euclidean metric manifolds or Asymmetric FlyHash (Section 4) for directional semantic embeddings. ## 3 The Holo-NN Retrieval Architecture ### 3.1 Feature Projections & Shared Feature Space (F,G) Given database points \(t_i\in T\) and query _q_, the client and server apply complementary localized feature mappings \(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}:\mathbb{R}^D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^B\) (instantiated via RFF or Asymmetric FlyHash as detailed in Section 4). These mappings are constructed to satisfy two properties: (1) _Metric Locality_, preserving local neighborhood similarity \(\langle\mathcal{G}(t_i),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle\approx\text{sim}(q,t_i)\), and (2) _Zero-Mean Background Incoherence_, where global mean-centering \((\mathcal{G}(t_i)\leftarrow\mathcal{G}(t_i)-\mu)\) ensures that background inner products vanish in expectation \((\mathbb{E}[\langle\mathcal{G}(t_j),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle]=0)\). Stacking the _N_ transformed database vectors produces the database embedding matrix: \(G=\mathcal{G}(T)=\left[\begin{array}{ c } \mathcal{G}(t_1)^T \\ \mathcal{G}(t_2)^T \\ \vdots \\ \mathcal{G}(t_N)^T \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times B}\) (13) The uncompressed affinity vector \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) between query _q_ and all _N_ database points is: \(s=G\mathcal{F}(q)=\left[\begin{array}{ c } \langle\mathcal{G}(t_1),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle \\ \vdots \\ \langle\mathcal{G}(t_N),\mathcal{F}(q)\rangle \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^N\) (14) Because F and G act as localized spatial or angular bandpass filters, _s_ is _k_eff_-compressible_ (approximately sparse): its _k_eff largest positive components capture the local Voronoi neighborhood around _q_, while the residual background tail decays rapidly below the universal soft-thresholding floor \(\lambda\). ### 3.2 Offline Server Database Grating Rather than storing or scanning \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times B}\) at query time, the server pre-multiplies the database feature matrix with the pseudorandom measurement matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}\): \(H=AG=A\mathcal{G}(T)\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times B}\) (15) The resulting matrix _H_ is the **Holographic Sensing Matrix**. It compresses the _N_-point database into _M_ linear measurement channels across the _B_ feature dimensions. This computation is executed strictly **offline**, once, during index construction and stored permanently on the server. Given the offline pre-computation of _H_, the function of the server benefits from theoretical or empirical optimization on algorithm parameters and hash choice. Further, because this computation is embarrassingly parallel, it can be seamlessly partitioned and executed in batch or form the basis for hierarchical design as needed. ### 3.3 Non-Interactive Linear Query Evaluation (_y=H_F(_q_)) At query time, the client computes its _B_-dimensional feature representation F(_q_) locally and transmits it to the server (either in sparse-plaintext for bandwidth- constrained ANN, or encrypted under a Linearly Homomorphic Encryption scheme as detailed in Section 6). The server then executes a single linear matrix-vector evaluation: \(y=H\mathcal{F}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^M\) (16) By association: \(y=H\mathcal{F}(q)=(AG)\mathcal{F}(q)=A(G\mathcal{F}(q))=As\) (17)

<tbc>The server thus produces the exact Compressive Sensing measurement vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^M\) of the latent sparse similarity signal \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\), without ever materializing or inspecting the full _N_-dimensional vector _s_. Crucially, because the server operator _H_ is strictly linear, cryptographic deployment does not require deep Fully Homomorphic Encryption or bootstrapping; any Linearly Homomorphic Encryption (LHE) or Ring-LWE SIMD scheme suffices to evaluate \(y=H\cdot\text{Enc}(\mathcal{F}(q))\) directly over ciphertexts.

### 3.4 Client Enclave Sparse Recovery & Candidate Reranking

Upon receiving the _M_-dimensional measurement vector _y_, the client recovers the sparse similarity vector \(\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}^N\) by solving the non-negative \(\ell_1\)-regularized inverse problem (LASSO \[42\]):

\(\hat{s}=argmin_{s\ge 0}\frac{1}{2}\left\|As-y\right\|_2^2+\lambda\left\|s\right\|_1\) (18)

The client solves this convex optimization problem locally (or within a secure enclave) using any popular sparse recovery algorithm, such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) \[43\], Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding (ISTA) \[21\], or the GPU-accelerated **Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA)** \[6\] as we do in this work:

\(u^{(k)}=z^{(k)}-\frac{1}{L}A^T\left(Az^{(k)}-y\right)\) (19)

\(s^{(k+1)}=\mathcal{S}_{\lambda/L}\left(u^{(k)}\right)=max\left(0,u^{(k)}-\frac{\lambda}{L}\right)\) (20)

\(t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}}{2}\) (21)

\(z^{(k+1)}=s^{(k+1)}+\frac{t_k-1}{t_{k+1}}\left(s^{(k+1)}-s^{(k)}\right)\) (22)

with initial conditions _s_<sup>(0)</sup>=_z_<sup>(1)</sup>=0_,t_<sub>1</sub>=1, Bai-Yin spectral step size \(L=\left\|A^TA\right\|_2\approx(1+\sqrt{N_\text{block}/M_\text{block}})^2\) \[46\], and Donoho-Johnstone universal threshold \(\lambda=\frac{1}{M_\text{block}}\sqrt{2N_\text{block}lnN_\text{block}/D}\) \[23\].

Upon convergence, the client extracts the top _K_<sup>∗</sup> coordinates with the highest recovered affinity scores:

\(\text{Top-}K^*(\hat{s})\subset\{1,2,\dots,N\}\) (23)

When only candidate IDs are required (or when the client caches lightweight metadata locally), retrieval terminates here in a single round trip. When full record payloads or exact metric reranking over the _K_<sup>∗</sup> candidates is required, the client issues a secondary Private Information Retrieval (Batch PIR, e.g., via HintlessPIR \[31\]) re-query for those _K_<sup>∗</sup> indices and computes exact distances locally without revealing the candidate support to the server.

### 3.5 Offline Index Tuning & Data- Dependent Operating Curves

In practice, the dimensions _M_ (measurement count), _B_ (feature embedding width), and _K_<sup>∗</sup> (candidate verification budget) establish an operational tradeoff between accuracy, communication bandwidth, and computation. While Compressive Sensing theory establishes that _M_ scales logarithmically with ambient dimension for a fixed sparsity level \((M=\mathcal{O}(k_\text{eff}ln(\frac{N}{k_\text{eff}}))\) \[24, 25\]), the effective sparsity _k_eff of the affinity vector _s_=G(_T_)F(_q_)--and the magnitude of background cross-talk across non-neighbors-- is inherently _data- and manifold-dependent_, varying with intrinsic dimensionality, metric concentration, and kernel bandwidth.

Crucially, because the holographic grating _H=A_G(_T_) is constructed offline on the server, with the full database _T_ in hand, Holo-NN requires no brittle closed-form heuristics to guess _M_ or _K_<sup>∗</sup> in the blind. Much like tuning graph degree or probe budgets (e.g., `efSearch` \[35\], `nprobe` \[30, 28\]) in traditional plaintext ANN indices, the index operator has ample offline compute during index construction to profile recall across a validation query split and select the exact (_M,B,K_<sup>∗</sup>) operating point along the dataset’s empirical bandwidth-accuracy Pareto curve.

## 4 Asymmetric Neural Hashing & Geometric Duality

### 4.1 The Double-Quantization Pathology in Symmetric Sparse Coding

High-dimensional semantic vectors (such as word embeddings and neural sentence representations) reside on continuous manifolds where continuous kernel functions often suffer from high-density concentration. To create sparse anchor representations, neural hashing algorithms draw inspiration from biological olfactory circuits \[20\], projecting inputs from low-dimensional projection neurons into an expanded Kenyon cell layer (\(B\gg D\)) and applying winner-take-all (_k_-WTA) competitive inhibition.

In conventional symmetric sparse coding, both the database points and the query vector are pruned to an identical top-_k_ active anchor budget (\(k_\text{db}=k_q\checkmark B\)). However, symmetric hard sparsification induces a severe **double-quantization pathology**: if a salient anchor ranks just above the top-_k_ cutoff in a database vector but falls slightly below the cutoff in the query vector, their dot product vanishes completely. This sharp thresholding causes false-negative dropouts across high-dimensional semantic benchmarks.

To circumvent this limitation in compressed sensing environments, we apply an **Asymmetric FlyHash (AFH)**, breaking the symmetry between database encoding and query representation. In this approach, the functions applied to query F and database G are different, with the<tbc>

<tbc>latter being significantly sparser than the former:

1. **Database Grating (**\(k_\mathrm{db}\checkmark B\)**)**: The server’s precomputed database feature representation \(G=\mathcal{G}(T)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times B}\) maintains a strict, ultra-sparse support (\(k_\mathrm{db}\checkmark B\) per row). This ensures that the offline holographic matrix \(H=AG\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times B}\) remains compact and computationally efficient.<tbc>

2. **Query Aperture (**_k<sub>q</sub>\>k_<sub>db</sub>**)**: The client projects the query _q_ through a broader activation aperture (\(k_q=\alpha_\mathrm{aperture}\cdot k_\mathrm{db}\) with \(\alpha_\mathrm{aperture}>1\)).

Opening the query aperture is free in bandwidth terms across both plaintext and encrypted deployments. In plaintext, transmission communicates only the non-zero coordinates of F(_q_), so cost grows with _k<sub>q</sub>_ from a negligible base. Under homomorphic encryption, the query is a _dense SIMD ciphertext_ spanning all _B_ slots whose byte size depends only on _B_ and the RNS limb count and is therefore completely independent of _k<sub>q</sub>_--transmitting only the active coordinates is not an option, since the support of F(_q_) must remain hidden from the server. In both regimes, the broad query aperture allows all potentially relevant semantic dimensions while the server’s sharp database grating acts as a spatial filter, eliminating false-negative dropouts with no additional communication overhead.

### 4.2 Geometric Duality: Continuous Euclidean RFF vs. Discrete Hyperplane Competition

Empirical and theoretical investigations reveal idiosyncratic, data-dependent structures governing feature transform selection. That is, while arguments for _a priori_ parameter selection can be made, the dominating influences on the parameter choices for a dataset come from the structure, distribution and density of the data manifold, in addition to its ambient dimension _D_. MNIST-784 (_D_=784) falls squarely in the first regime while GloVe-25 (_D_=25) falls squarely in the second, as _D_ alone does not predict which transform applies.

1. **Spatially Structured Metric Manifolds (low intrinsic dimension)**: In Euclidean metric spaces with physical or spatial structure (e.g., 2D spatial seeds, MNIST-784 pixel spaces, and SIFT-128 image descriptors), pairwise Euclidean distances show meaningful local contrast. In this regime, Random Fourier Features (RFF) with Gaussian RBF kernels \(K(x,y)=\mathrm{exp}(-\gamma\|x-y\|_2^2)\) create genuine physical sparsity because spatial volume scales as O(_r<sup>D</sup>_). Points outside the local kernel radius \(r>3/\sqrt{2\gamma}\) decay exponentially toward zero, enabling high-fidelity metric nearest neighbor recovery (Figure 2 and  1).<tbc>

2. **Unstructured Semantic Hyerspheres (intrinsic dimension** ≈**ambient** _D_**)**: On unconstrained<tbc>

<tbc>hyperspherical manifolds, pairwise Euclidean distances concentrate sharply around \(\sqrt{2}\) as _D_ grows, since \(\|x-y\|_2^2=2-2\langle x,y\rangle\) and \(\langle x,y\rangle\rightarrow 0\) by measure concentration on the sphere. Continuous exponential kernels suffer from amplitude collapse, where the true neighbor similarity signal drops below the finite-sample RFF Monte Carlo noise floor \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{B})\).

In contrast, Asymmetric FlyHash partitions high- dimensional space via nearly orthogonal random hyperplanes. Discrete _k_-WTA competition creates implicit Voronoi cells, preserving semantic locality without exponential amplitude attenuation and remaining robust to the curse of dimensionality. Moreover, because feature strength is preserved within each Voronoi cell, a local "in-cell Euclidean metric" breaks ties and further increases NN accuracy.

## 6 Encrypted Retrieval System Implementation & SOTA Comparison

Holo-NN is designed for blind cloud retrieval across four complementary Ring-LWE encrypted execution backends: (1) exact-integer BFV homomorphic matrix-vector evaluation via Google’s **HintlessPIR / LinPIR** engine \[31\], (2) depth-1 modulus-switched approximate homomorphic encryption on CPU via **OpenFHE** \[1\] under the Cheon- Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) scheme \[16\] compiled through **HEIR** \[3\], (3) 64-bit RNS GPU-accelerated CKKS evaluation on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU (24 GB VRAM) via **Phantom** \[45\] with a fused 128-bit lazy-<tbc>

<tbc>reduction BSGS inner-product kernel, and (4) 32-bit RNS double-hoisted GPU CKKS evaluation on a single RTX 3090 GPU (and NVIDIA H100) lowered via **HEIR** \[3\] to **Cheddar** \[17\].

The encrypted retrieval pipeline executes via a strictly linear four-step protocol:

1. **Offline Precomputation (Server)**: The server computes the holographic index \(H=AG=\mathcal{AG}(T)\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times B}\) once across all database embeddings and pre- encodes its diagonals in NTT evaluation form.<tbc>

2. **Query Encryption (Client)**: The client lifts query \(q\rightarrow\mathcal{F}(q)\) and encrypts Enc(F(_q_)) into SIMD ciphertext slots.<tbc>

3. **Blind Linear Evaluation (Server)**: The server evaluates \(\mathrm{Enc}(y)=H\cdot\mathrm{Enc}(\mathcal{F}(q))\) via diagonal NTT plaintext-ciphertext multiplication with zero bootstrapping--using single-generator cyclic query rotations and rotation-free row accumulation under LinPIR, or Baby-Step Giant-Step (BSGS) evaluation followed by single-limb modulus switching (`Compress`) under CKKS.<tbc>

4. **Client Recovery & Optional PIR Reranking**: The client decrypts _y_=Dec(Enc(_y_)) locally, reconstructs sparse coefficients \(\hat{s}=\text{FISTA}(y,A,\lambda,L)\) and extracts the top _K_<sup>∗</sup> candidate IDs (issuing an optional secondary Batch PIR re-query for those _K_<sup>∗</sup> records when exact-distance reranking or document payloads are needed; Section 3.4).

### 6.1 Degree-1 Blind Linear Arithmetic & Compiler Optimizations

Prior FHE-based vector search systems evaluate non-linear Euclidean distances or polynomial approximations of cosine similarity under homomorphic encryption. Evaluating polynomial approximations of degree \(d\ge 12\) requires deep homomorphic circuits, inducing large noise growth that necessitates expensive **FHE bootstrapping** operations (often requiring 10-60 seconds per ciphertext).

In Holo-NN, the server’s blind evaluation is strictly linear:

\(\mathrm{Enc}(y)=H\cdot\mathrm{Enc}(\mathcal{F}(q))\) (24)

Because _H_ is plaintext and Enc(F(_q_)) is a degree-1 ciphertext, the server executes only homomorphic plaintext- ciphertext multiplications, additions, and slot rotations:

• **Multiplicative Depth**: Exactly **1** (Degree-1 linear operator).<tbc>

• **FHE Bootstrapping**: **0 bootstrapping operations** required throughout the entire query lifecycle.<tbc>

• **Compiler Optimization via HEIR**: Lowering the matrix-vector multiplication through the MLIR-based<tbc>

HEIR compiler \[3\] automatically synthesizes diagonal ciphertext rotations and hoists plaintext weights, yielding optimal SIMD slot packing across OpenFHE backends.<tbc>

• **Noise Growth**: Minimal invariant noise budget, permitting compact RLWE parameter sets at OpenFHE’s `HEStd\_128\_classic` security standard \[2\] (_N_ring=16,384 for 8,192-slot blocks and _N_ring=32,768 for 16,384-slot blocks).<tbc>

Two caveats govern how that table should be read. The two conventions diverge sharply, and the divergence is informative. At _M_=300,000 Holo-NN locates _the_ nearest neighbor within its top ten for 93.0% of queries, but recovers only 61.6% of each query’s _ten_ nearest neighbors in that same top ten. The missing neighbors have not been lost: raising the cutoff to fifty recovers 92.0% of them, from a candidate set that is still \(20,000\times\) smaller than the database.

The gap is also strikingly persistent in _M_. Over the sweep, 1-recall@10 climbs from 63.4% to 98.5% and is effectively saturated by _M_=500,000, whereas 10-recall@10 moves only from 33.3% to 73.0% and is still rising roughly linearly when 1-recall has flattened. Adding measurements sharpens the question "is the true nearest neighbor in this list" long before it sharpens "are these ten the right ten". A budget that resolves the first question almost perfectly leaves the second one a quarter unanswered.

This is the expected behavior of \(\ell_1\) recovery on a correlated support, not a defect of the measurement operator. A query’s ten true nearest neighbors are, by construction, mutually near-identical, so their feature vectors G(_t<sub>i</sub>_) are highly correlated and the corresponding columns of _H=A_G(_T_) are nearly collinear. Faced with a group of near-collinear atoms that jointly explain the measurement,<tbc>

<tbc>the LASSO \[42\] does not distribute the coefficient across the group; it concentrates the mass on a single representative and shrinks the remainder toward zero \[50\]. The surviving representative is reliably _a_ member of the true neighbor set -- which is why 1-recall is high -- while its near-duplicates are demoted in magnitude though not eliminated, which is why they reappear as the cutoff widens.

The implication is that Holo-NN, in its present form, is best understood as an unusually cheap, tunable, high- coverage approximate nearest-neighbor algorithm rather than a precise ranker, even in the limit of computation and bandwidth. Where a downstream exact-distance stage is available -- a client that already holds the candidate payloads, or a private retrieval step as in Section 3.4 -- the relevant quantity is the coverage figure, and 92.0% of the true ten neighbors for 5.37 MB in 0.82s (HEIR- GPU CKKS), 11.13 MB (64-bit CKKS), or 265.4 MB with zero persistent server state (LinPIR) in one round trip compares favorably with Panther’s 88.85% for 92.9 MB and SANNS’s ≈90% for 1.77 GB -- though the comparison is not strict, since SANNS and Panther deliver their top-ten sets already ranked within a top ten while Holo-NN is a top fifty, awaiting a reranking stage. Where no such stage exists, the ranking Holo-NN emits is materially weaker than Compass’s. Substituting an Elastic Net \[50\] (\(\ell_1+\ell_2\)) or Group LASSO \[47\] proximal operator for the \(\ell_1\) soft threshold would be expected to redistribute mass across correlated groups and close much of this gap, at no cost in bandwidth, round trips or server work, since it changes only the client’s local recovery step. We leave this to future work.

## 7 Conclusion

We presented **Holo-NN**, a holographic approximate nearest neighbor retrieval architecture that reformulates nearest neighbor search as an underdetermined linear Compressive Sensing problem. By precomputing a degree-1 compressed database representation offline (\(H=AG=A\mathcal{G}(T)\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times B}\)), Holo-NN executes blind, privacy- preserving retrieval via a single linear operator requiring \(M\checkmark N\) measurements in a single non-interactive round trip, with no client-side index state and no pre- processing stream. Because _H_ is constructed offline on the server, the index operator can profile the empirical bandwidth-recall trade-off directly on the target dataset, while our Asymmetric FlyHash projection removes the double-quantization loss that a symmetric sparse code would incur on high-dimensional semantic manifolds.

Holo-NN works in plaintext as a generic high-confidence, approximate nearest neighbor algorithm. Because blind forms of the algorithm function as single-round private linear operations, they scale well to LinPIR or other private linear operations while retaining naturally scalable, embarrassingly parallel computational models that are well suited to modern hardware.
